THE SHORT VERSION

What are the seven deadly sins?

The seven deadly sins are a traditional Christian grouping of vices. The Catholic Catechism lists pride, avarice, envy, wrath, lust, gluttony, and sloth or acedia. In everyday English, avarice is commonly called greed. The familiar names come from that ethical tradition; our characters and questions are our own interpretation.

Here, the names act as prompts for noticing habits: seeking recognition, wanting more, following a spark, comparing, overdoing, reacting, or postponing. The test is for entertainment and self-reflection. It does not determine whether someone is a good person or evaluate their religious life.

Source for the traditional list: Catechism of the Catholic Church, paragraph 1866.

THE WHOLE CAST

Seven names.
Seven different pulls.

The short questions below are reading prompts, not additional scored items.

Recognition

Pride

The Main Character

Pride traditionally describes placing your own importance above others and resisting correction. Confidence and pleasure in good work are not automatically pride.

In our quiz: Being seen as capable, important, or right.

What happens when someone corrects me?
Read the pride guide
Getting and keeping

Greed

The Treasure Keeper

Greed traditionally means an excessive attachment to wealth, possessions, or gain. Saving money or seeking security is not, by itself, greed.

In our quiz: Wanting another advantage, upgrade, or reserve.

Does enough keep moving after I reach a goal?
Read the greed guide
Attraction

Lust

The Spark Chaser

Lust traditionally concerns sexual desire when it overwhelms judgment or regard for other people. This quiz uses non-explicit questions about attraction and impulse; it is not an assessment of sexuality.

In our quiz: Letting a new spark take over attention and choices.

Am I following chemistry before considering what I want?
Read the lust guide
Comparison

Envy

The Side-Eye Scout

Envy traditionally describes distress at another person’s good fortune. Admiration, ambition, and noticing inequality are not automatically envy.

In our quiz: Measuring my situation against someone else’s good fortune.

Did their good news change how I feel about my own life?
Read the envy guide
The extra

Gluttony

The Just-One-More

Gluttony traditionally refers to excess in eating and drinking. The quiz also uses modern overconsumption as a playful analogy. It does not evaluate body size, eating disorders, or health.

In our quiz: Continuing to consume after enjoyment starts to fade.

Am I still enjoying this, or simply continuing?
Read the gluttony guide
The reaction

Wrath

The Tiny Volcano

Wrath traditionally means anger that becomes excessive, vengeful, or destructive. Anger itself is an ordinary emotion, and setting boundaries is not a failing.

In our quiz: Replying sharply, escalating, or wanting to get even.

Am I explaining a concern or trying to make it sting?
Read the wrath guide
The delay

Sloth

The Cozy Strategist

Sloth traditionally concerns neglect of meaningful responsibilities. Rest, disability, burnout, and depression are not moral failings; this entertainment quiz cannot distinguish or assess them.

In our quiz: Putting off a manageable responsibility until it grows.

What am I waiting for before taking the first step?

THE DIFFERENCES MATTER

Similar moments.
Different questions.

Pride and envy

Pride in this quiz asks how you respond to recognition and correction. Envy asks how someone else’s advantage changes the way you see your own situation. An overlooked contribution and a friend’s milestone may feel similar, but they are different prompts.

Greed and gluttony

Greed focuses on obtaining or keeping more. Gluttony uses continuing past enjoyment as its theme. Wanting another upgrade and mindlessly extending an activity can overlap without being the same habit.

Wrath and ordinary anger

The wrath questions explore sharp replies and extending conflict. Feeling angry, explaining a concern, or setting a boundary does not automatically fit that pattern.

Sloth and needed rest

The sloth questions describe postponement. They cannot identify why starting is difficult. Rest, limited capacity, and circumstances belong in the picture; the label cannot replace that context.

CHARACTERS, NOT VERDICTS

Use the label as a starting point.

A name can make a familiar habit easier to talk about, but it leaves out the situation around it. Someone can enjoy recognition, value financial security, feel attraction, and need rest without those experiences being failings.

Read all seven scores together. If one leads, explore the situations behind it. If several tie, keep the tie. Our results guide explains three example profiles, while the method page shows exactly how answers become numbers.

GOOD QUESTIONS

A little more context.

Is this a religious assessment?

No. The names have a religious history, but this original entertainment quiz asks about everyday situations. It does not evaluate faith, religious obligations, or moral standing.

Is this about The Seven Deadly Sins anime?

No. Our seven illustrated characters are original creations for this site. The quiz does not match you to anime characters.

Can more than one sin fit me?

Yes. The quiz scores seven tendencies independently. Several can be high, several can be low, and equal highest scores remain a tied result.
